Executive Summary: This project evaluated the capability of advanced inverter-based resources (IBRs) to provide essential reliability grid services through coordinated operation of grid- forming (GFM) and grid-following (GFL) technologies at the 380-MW Wheatridge hybrid facility. Budget Period 1 (BP1) focused on reducing technical risk and establishing the analytical, modeling, and engineering basis required for future field demonstration of GFM wind and GFM battery storage operating alongside GFL wind and solar. The project developed a structured set of GFM performance metrics that characterize angle support, voltage stiffness, frequency response, damping behavior, and current-limiting performance. These metrics established a consistent technical framework for evaluating GFM behavior under both disturbance and steady-state conditions and are directly applicable to future utility-scale deployments. Comprehensive electromagnetic transient (EMT) studies were conducted to validate expected GFM behavior prior to field implementation. These studies assessed mixed GFM/GFL interactions, weak-grid performance, phase-angle disturbances, voltage depressions, and multi-resource dynamics. Additional validation using planning models and a reduced-order “play-in” environment confirmed the consistency of key GFM response characteristics across model types. Results showed that properly Page 2 of 36 Award Number: DE-EE0010651 Recipient Name: Portland General Electric tuned GFM controls provide improved stability margins, enhanced voltage and frequency support, and reduced sensitivity to variations in grid strength. Complementary engineering activities supported technical readiness for future demonstration. These included development of a 30-mode Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA), preparation of GFM control-tuning approaches, engineering design reviews, preliminary commissioning procedures, measurement- system installation, and establishment of data-acquisition pathways. High-fidelity EMT models, plant-level control integrations, and initial hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing were completed, forming a validated modeling and simulation foundation for subsequent system-level testing. The BP1 results demonstrate that GFM inverters, when properly parameterized and validated, have the potential to improve system strength, provide fast and stable dynamic support, and enhance hybrid-plant performance under challenging grid conditions. The methodologies, models, and engineering processes established in BP1 provide a replicable framework for future GFM deployment and reduce uncertainty associated with large-scale hybrid-plant integration.
